source.title: The Strong Convergence of Subgradients of Convex Functions Along Directions: Perspectives and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let f: R^n -> R be a convex function with n >= 2, and let x(t) = (t, 0, ..., 0). Assume that the gradient ∇f(x(t)) exists for every t > 0. Must the one-sided limit lim_{t↓0} ∇f(x(t)) exist, or can one construct a convex function for which this directional limit of gradients fails to exist?

evidence.quote: Let f : Rn −→ R, with n ≥ 2, be a convex function, and set x (t) := (t, 0,..., 0) ∈ Rn , with t ∈ R. Assume that ∇ f (x(t)) exists for every t > 0, and consider the following limit: lim t↓0 ∇ f (x(t)). (1) We conjecture that the above limit may not exist. Hence, however , the question is still open.

accepted.question_text: Let f: R^n -> R be convex, let x(t) = (t, 0, ..., 0), and assume in addition that the Hessian Hf(x(t)) exists for all t > 0. Can the one-sided limit lim_{t↓0} Hf(x(t)) fail to exist? The paper explicitly treats this as an open second-order analogue of the directional gradient question, and also notes analogous infinite-dimensional and higher-order variants.
accepted.context_brief: Directional Hessian convergence along a ray

evidence.quote: F. Giannessi asked also several “second-order” questions. Namely, assuming additionally that Hessian Hf (x(t)) exists for all t > 0, where Hf (x(t)) stands for the Hessian of f at x(t), he asked whether: the limit lim t↓0 Hf (x(t)); (2)
might not exist. Infinite dimensional as well as higher order and other cases of this question can be considered.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a convex function f: R^2 -> R that is twice differentiable in a neighborhood of the origin but whose Hessian Hf(x) has no limit as x -> 0? This is proposed as the natural finite-dimensional starting case for the broader open problem about loss of Hessian convergence for convex functions.
accepted.context_brief: Twice-differentiable planar convex function with no Hessian limit

evidence.quote: It seems that an investigation might start with looking for an answer to the following question: does there exist a convex function f from R2 to R, derivable two times around the origin, for which the limit lim x→ 0 Hf (x) does not exist?

accepted.question_text: Let (X, ||·||) be a normed space, let f: X -> R ∪ {+∞} be convex, let x ∈ X and a nonzero direction w ∈ X be fixed, and assume that f is continuous on some open convex neighborhood U of x. For the directional family of convex-analytic subdifferentials ∂f(x + t w), when does the set-valued limit lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) exist?

evidence.quote: Let (X,∥·∥ ) be a normed space and f : X −→ R ∪{ + ∞ }be a convex function, x ∈ X , w ∈ X \{ 0} be fixed and U be an open convex set such that x ∈ U and f |U is continuous ... Consider the following limit: lim t↓0 ∂f (x + tw), (3) ... Let us ask basic questions (see questions following (1) too): when does the limit in (3) exist?

accepted.question_text: In the same setting of a convex function f on a normed space and a fixed point x, is there at least one nonzero direction w for which the directional subdifferential limit lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) exists?
accepted.context_brief: Existence of at least one good direction

evidence.quote: Let us ask basic questions (see questions following (1) too): when does the limit in (3) exist? Is there any direction for which the limit exists?

accepted.question_text: For a convex function f on a normed space and a fixed point x, is the set of nonzero directions w for which the directional subdifferential limit lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) exists dense in the ambient space?

evidence.quote: Is the set of “good” directions, for which the convergence holds true, dense in the space?

accepted.question_text: Given a convex function f for which directional subgradient convergence is under study, can one obtain positive existence results for lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) after only a small perturbation of the function? Equivalently, does a sufficiently small perturbation preserve directional convergence of subgradients along a dense subset of directions?

evidence.quote: Can we provide positive answers to the questions on the limit in (3) by a little change of the function under consideration (in other words, does a small perturbation preserve the directional convergence of subgradients along a dense subset of directions?)?

accepted.question_text: For which nonzero directions w does the directional subdifferential limit lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) exist as a singleton rather than as a larger set? The paper singles this out as a particularly demanding version of the directional convergence problem.

evidence.quote: we should also add the following question: for which directions is the limit, in (3), a singleton? Perhaps this question is the most demanding and will require a lot of work to be elaborated properly.

accepted.question_text: Let H be a real Hilbert space and let f: H -> R be a continuous convex function such that for every x in H the subdifferential ∂f(x) contains at least one unit vector. Suppose that at some point x̄ the set ∂f(x̄) ∩ S_H[0,1] consists of exactly one unit subgradient {x̄*}. Must f then be Gâteaux differentiable at x̄?
accepted.context_brief: Unique unit subgradient versus Gateaux differentiability

evidence.quote: Let H be a real Hilbert space and f : H −→ R be a continuous convex function such that ∂f (x) ∩ SH[0, 1] ̸=∅ for all x ∈ H ... Suppose that for a given ¯x ∈ H the set ∂f (¯x) ∩ SH[0, 1] is a singleton, say {¯x∗}= ∂f (¯x) ∩ SH[0, 1]. Does it imply that the Gâteaux derivative, DG f (¯x), exists?

accepted.question_text: Let Q be a subset of a Hilbert space H such that every point of H has a unique farthest point in Q. Must Q be a singleton? The paper presents this as V. Klee's still-open farthest-point problem and explains that a sufficiently strong positive result on directional convergence of subgradients would resolve it.

evidence.quote: A good example, where the directional convergence of subgradients would work effectively, is the problem by V . Klee— it is still open ; see [4]—suppose Q is a subset of Hilbert space H such that each point of H admits a unique farthest point in Q . Must Q consist of a single point?

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to construct a continuous convex function f on a separable Hilbert space such that, at every point x where the Gâteaux derivative D_G f(x) exists, the set of directions along which the directional convergence of subgradients holds is not dense in the space?
accepted.context_brief: Separable Hilbert example with non-dense good directions

evidence.quote: Thus we should ask: is it possible to construct a convex continuous function f on a separable Hilbert space such that for every point x , where the Gâteaux derivative exists, say DG f (x), the set of directions for which the directional convergence of subgradients holds true, is not dense in the space?

accepted.question_text: Does every continuous convex function on a separable Hilbert space admit a second-order Gâteaux expansion at at least one point, or perhaps on a dense set of points? The paper identifies this as Jonathan Borwein's especially intriguing open question about convex functions in infinite dimensions.

evidence.quote: If we were able to construct such a function, then ( 5) would not be satisfied ... and consequently it would be an answer in the negative to the question, which we find in [ 1], that is to the question: Does every continuous convex function on separable Hilbert space admit a second-order Gâteaux expansion at at least one point (or perhaps on a dense set of points)?

accepted.question_text: Fix a direction w_0 and a tolerance ε > 0. For a given convex continuous function f and point x, can one find a nearby direction w with ||w_0 - w|| < ε and another convex continuous function g_ε such that |f(y) - f(x)| <= |g_ε(y) - g_ε(x)| + ε ||y - x|| for all y in X, and such that the directional subdifferential limit lim_{t↓0} ∂g_ε(x + t w) exists?
accepted.context_brief: Nearby perturbation and nearby direction question

evidence.quote: For example, fix a direction w0 and ϵ> 0 as small as we need. It would be valuable to know if there are directions w such that that ∥w0 − w∥ <ϵ and a convex continuous function, say gϵ , such that ∀y ∈ X,| f (y) − f (x)|≤| gϵ(y) − gϵ(x)|+ ϵ∥y − x∥ (13) and the limit lim t↓0 ∂gϵ(x + tw) (14) exists;

accepted.question_text: Is there a continuous convex function on a Hilbert space for which, at some point x, the directional subdifferential limit lim_{t↓0} ∂f(x + t w) fails to exist for every direction w in some nonempty open subset of directions?
accepted.context_brief: Failure of directional convergence on an open set of directions

evidence.quote: Finally, let us pose the following question; see questions following ( 3): is there a convex continuous function defined on a Hilbert space such that, for some x , the limit in (3) does not exist for some nonempty open subset of directions?

needs_review.question_text_raw: At this moment, it is unknown whether an example of a convex continuous function on a Hilbert space, such that the limits in (10) do not exist for all directions from a dense Gδ subset, can be provided—it is an open question.
